Close lhirlimann's Diary Capitole du Libre 2026 Posted by lhirlimann on 15 November 2026 in French (Français) . Hier soir, j’ai présenté dans l’amphithéâtre C002 au sein du campus de enseeiht à Toulouse, « Contribuez à OSM ». La bonne surprise fut le taux de remplissage de la salle. J’ai compté plus d’une vingtaine de personnes. La présentation était articulée en deux parties : la première, un tout petit peu de théorie et pas de présentation d’outils ; la deuxième, des démonstrations, des petits trucs faciles pour commencer, puis des trucs plus « grands » (de l’infrastructure). En trente minutes, j’avais plié ma présentation. Il restait vingt-cinq minutes, qui se sont très, très facilement remplies par de très nombreuses questions. Merci au plublic pour ces questions. Merci à l’organisation du Capitole du Libre. La présentation est disponible à https://files.hirlimann.net/talks/cdl2026/ . Location: Les Chalets / Bayard / Belfort / Saint-Aubin / Dupuy, Toulouse, Haute-Garonne, Occitanie, France métropolitaine, France Discussion Leave a comment Log in to leave a comment

Library and information science is a field of study that encompasses all of the aspects of the creation, organization, documentation, management, communication, and use of recorded information. It is the umbrella term for a wide variety of fields of study and work, including librarianship, information management, knowledge management, archiving, and records management, and is tangential to museum studies. The Zawiya refinery, west of the capital Tripoli, was hit in a drone strike on Monday evening - the third such incident in two days. The National Oil Corporation (NOC) said a tank containing about 4.5m litres of fuel was directly hit, triggering a huge fire that caused it to collapse. It said it was considering suspending operations if the attacks continued. There were no "serious injuries" from the fire, with most patients treated for smoke inhalation, Libya's Ambulance and Emergency Service said on Tuesday. The Zawiya refinery is the largest operational facility in Libya, with an output of 120,000 barrels per day. The NOC condemned similar attacks in past days in Zawiya, including two drone strikes on a naphtha reservoir and a water desalination plant. It called on the authorities to investigate who was behind the violence. The attacks have highlighted continuing instability in Libya, which has been split in two since a civil war broke out after the ousting of former leader Muammar Gaddafi. I could finally relax," says Abdulwahab Damdoum, surveying his luxurious new apartment overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in the eastern Libyan city of Derna. Just three years ago he was clinging in terror to the roof of a house as the world's deadliest flood this century surged around him. Now the 27-year-old port worker, his wife and two young daughters have been given a new, free, 300-sq-m home in a showcase development commissioned by a son of Khalifa Haftar, the warlord who controls eastern Libya. It is part of a rapid $2bn (£1.5bn) rebuilding of Derna that the powerful Haftar family hope will serve as a model for development throughout Libya, increasing their influence across a country currently split between east and west, with rival governments in charge. The money comes from the state coffers of the oil-rich country, allocated by its parliament. But there are no published records of how it has been spent, raising questions about accountability and possible corruption. pages.text: Light pollution is getting worse, and Earth is paying the price | National Geographic By Nadia Drake Photographs by Babak Tafreshi Published April 3, 2019 • 25 min read On a clear night in 1994, an earthquake rumbled beneath Los Angeles and caused a city-wide power outage just before dawn. Startled awake, some residents who had stumbled outside called various emergency centers and a local observatory to report a mysterious cloud overhead. That weird object turned out to be the band of the Milky Way , our home galaxy, which had long been obscured from view by the city’s lights. Arguably, the light bulb is the most transformative invention humans have introduced to this planet. By flicking a switch or pushing a button, we can push back the veil that would naturally shroud our lives each night. Now, we work long after the sun sinks below the horizon. We play games outside until the hours stretch into double digits. We more safely roam city streets after dark. ( Opinion: Bright Nights, Big Problems) The city of Las Vegas dumps an enormous amount of light into its environment, turning the night sky above into a seemingly blank canvas. Light Water Reactor Sustainability (LWRS) Program The Light Water Reactor Sustainability (LWRS) program conducts research to develop technologies and other solutions to improve the economics and reliability, sustain the safety, and extend the operation of our nation’s fleet of nuclear power plants. It has two objectives with respect to long-term operations: (1) to provide science- and technology-based solutions to industry to overcome the current labor-intensive business model and associated practices; and (2) to manage the aging of systems, structures, and components (SSCs) so nuclear power plants can continue to operate safely and cost-effectively. Photograph By Babak Tafreshi, Nat Geo Image Collection By National Geographic Staff Last updated July 21, 2025 Lightning flashing across a darkened sky makes an unforgettable image. With their drama and power, it’s no wonder people have infused them with symbolic meaning. They’re associated with mythological deities, such as Zeus and Thor, and even an emoji , in popular culture. In daily life, these electric currents can be dangerous, sparking intense forest fires and causing deaths. It doesn’t help that there are many myths about lightning behavior. From its causes to safety tips, here’s everything you need to know about these bolts from the blue. What is lightning and what causes it? Lightning is an electrical discharge caused by imbalances between storm clouds and the ground, or within the clouds themselves. Most occur within the clouds. During a storm, colliding particles of rain, ice, or snow inside storm clouds increase the imbalance between storm clouds and the ground, and often negatively charge the lower reaches of storm clouds. Petruska Abstract Linear motion components are widely used in antenna metrology positioning systems, but long motion ranges can reduce positioning accuracy due to the difficulty of eliminating rail component non-linearity. Listeria Outbreaks About these resources When two or more people get the same illness from the same contaminated food or drink, the event is called a foodborne disease outbreak. The list on this page primarily represents multistate foodborne outbreak investigations involving Listeria in the last two years where CDC was the lead public health agency. For a complete listing of reported outbreaks please use the National Outbreak Reporting System (NORS) Dashboard . Public health officials investigate outbreaks to control them, so more people do not get sick, and to learn how to prevent similar outbreaks from happening in the future. Efficient, cost-effective recovery and recycling of the critical minerals stored in these batteries helps the U.S. meet its objectives of sustaining domestic critical mineral supplies, developing energy independence, and moving into a circular economy. Introduction Lithium batteries are vital components in many everyday consumer products, such as cell phones and backup power storage units. They play a crucial role in the rapidly growing U.S. markets for vehicle manufacturing, energy storage, medical services, and agricultural technology. These batteries also may contain important minerals and materials, including lithium (Li), cobalt (Co), and nickel (Ni), which are essential for many technologies driving U.S. commerce. Efficient and cost-effective recovery and reuse of these critical minerals can help secure a domestic supply and support a transition away from a “linear economy,” where materials are extracted, manufactured into products, used, and then discarded. Credit: Megan King/NIST Four years ago, NIST researcher Cyrus Daugherty developed an algorithm to virtually unroll the tightly wrapped layers of a cylindrical lithium-ion battery. Daugherty’s software transformed X-ray images of the battery, taken at different angles, into a CT scan. The scan, a 3D portrait of the battery’s interior, pinpointed hard-to-spot defects and highlighted wear and tear on its electrodes. This study aims to extend the life of lithium-ion batteries , which power everything from laptops and cellphones to e-bikes and electric cars. LM Information Technology Specialist Kyle Brown accepted the award on LM’s behalf. The EPEAT award recognizes organizations for excellence in sustainable procurement of electronic equipment. EPEAT is a method for purchasers to evaluate a product’s effect on the environment, rate it accordingly, and identify it as a preferable electronic good. Manufacturers register products in the EPEAT category based on the device’s ability to meet certain criteria, including product lifestyle, design, energy production, and recycling. pages.text: Lobito Corridor: Can Trump-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo and Angola? Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Weather Newsletters Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo? 3 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Akisa Wandera BBC Africa, Lobito AFP via Getty Images The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments. She is thinking about getting around more easily. The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast. For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient. "Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says. But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport. It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo. Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development. Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi has alleged he was abducted by armed men and handed over "hooded and bound" to FBI agents, who had a plane waiting to fly him out of the country. Al-Marimi, also known as Mas'ud, has denied building and priming the bomb that brought down Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie on 21 December 1988, killing 270 people. The Libyan argues he was the victim of an unlawful rendition and has asked a judge in Washington DC to throw the case out of court. In response, the US Department of Justice said, under American law, the manner of his removal should not stop his thrice-postponed trial from finally getting underway in January. pages.text: Look for the 'Summer Triangle' Stars. They Can Unlock the Rest of the Night Sky. | National Geographic SCIENCE NIGHT SKY GUIDE Look for the 'Summer Triangle' Stars. They Can Unlock the Rest of the Night Sky. Made up of three of summer’s brightest stars, the Summer Triangle is an easy starting point for exploring—and photographing—the Milky Way and beyond. The Milky Way arcs above the walls of a gorge, framed by the three bright stars of the Summer Triangle. BABAK TAFRESHI, National Geographic Image Collection By Stefanie Waldek Published August 20, 2026 Stargazing can feel overwhelming when you don’t know where to begin. But in August, three exceptionally bright stars offer an easy starting point. Vega, Deneb, and Altair form the Summer Triangle, an enormous star pattern that rises high in the evening sky across much of the Northern Hemisphere. Once you find it, the triangle can serve as a guide to nearby constellations, deep-sky objects, and the Milky Way. It is also one of the most photogenic regions of the summer sky in August. Here’s how to find the Summer Triangle—and photograph what surrounds it. How to Find the Summer Triangle The Summer Triangle is not a constellation, but an asterism, or a recognizable pattern of stars. Begin with Vega, one of the brightest stars visible from Earth. In mid-August, observers in the Northern Hemisphere can generally find it high overhead. Deneb appears to one side of Vega, while Altair lies farther away, creating a large, elongated triangle. pages.description: On autumn evenings, Capella can put on a dazzling display of red, green, and blue. Here's why it happens and where to look.
pages.text: Look for This Colorful, Twinkling Star in the Night Sky This Fall | National Geographic SCIENCE NIGHT SKY GUIDE Look for This Colorful, Twinkling Star in the Night Sky This Fall On autumn evenings, Capella can put on a dazzling display of red, green, and blue. Here's why it happens and where to look. Venus, the Pleiades star cluster, and the bright star Capella rise in the dawn sky above a tufa formation in California’s Mono Lake. BABAK TAFRESHI, National Geographic Image Collection By Stefanie Waldek Published November 12, 2026 Look low in the northeastern sky on an autumn evening, and you might spot something unusual: a bright star flashing red, green, and blue. That’s Capella, one of the brightest stars in the night sky. But despite appearances, the star isn’t actually changing colors. The dazzling display is an optical effect caused by starlight passing through Earth’s atmosphere. And Capella isn’t the only star that puts on this kind of show. “Stars appear to twinkle or shimmer in the night sky, but this is not an inherent trait of stars,” says Emily Watson, astrophysicist and planetarium supervisor at the U.S. Space & Rocket Center. “As the light from a star passes through different densities and temperatures within our atmosphere, the light bends in a process called refraction.” The color flashes happen because Earth’s atmosphere bends different wavelengths of light by different degrees. pages.text: Los Mirlos: Tiny Desk Concert : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Los Mirlos: Tiny Desk Concert For more than 50 years, Los Mirlos has cultivated its own Peruvian twist on cumbia, featuring reverb-heavy, surf-rock guitar. Los Mirlos: Tiny Desk Concert September 17, 2026 10:00 AM ET Felix Contreras Credit: Photo: Vanessa Castillo/NPR From jazz and Tejano to norteño and ska, 'El Tiny' returns with a takeover from Sept. 15 to Oct. 15 for Latin Music Month . Originally born from Afro-Colombian communities, cumbia spread across the Spanish-speaking world , acquiring distinct musical accents along the way. In Peru, cumbia became particularly popular among oil workers deep in the Amazon. And when Jorge Rodriguez Grández started Los Mirlos in his small hometown of Moyobamba, his band played a regional style called cumbia amazónica, easily identifiable by its electric, reverb-heavy, surf-rock guitar. Sponsor Message Alt.Latino Cumbia: The Musical Backbone Of Latin America Los Mirlos' time behind the Desk is not only a joyful celebration of this music but also a trail of small towns and cities throughout the Amazon jungle. Throughout their performance, these cultural ambassadors share stories and declare their love for cumbia and their tropical homeland. We are so fortunate to host and share with you a group of true pioneers and innovators who, over 50 years later, still effortlessly pump out cumbia grooves. Los Texmaniacs ' music is a living history lesson. The conjunto sound is driven by the button accordion, a mid-19th century instrument that made its way to the U.S.-Mexico border by way of German, Czech and Polish immigrants. But this music is also just perfect for twirling on the dance floor to songs about true love, heartbreak, folk heroes and reflections on life. pages.text: Los Tigres' Tiny Desk, explained : Alt.Latino : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Los Tigres' Tiny Desk, explained : Alt.Latino Last week we published a Tiny Desk Concert that ended up being unusual for a few reasons. First of all, it was the final production of our sixth annual El Tiny series. This was a very emotional moment for a lot of reasons. People really love Los Tigres del Norte, to the point that playing their albums feels like sitting with family. And if you’ve seen the introduction I gave the band just before they played at the desk you can see that I wasn’t embarrassed to get emotional when I talked about what the band means to me. That emotional intro led to some changes in our process and format that resulted in a huge response from the audience that went viral. The result was a messy moment behind the scenes here at NPR and more than a little confusion for a lot of you. This week’s episode looks back at last week. First we want to share with you, directly from us, an explanation of what happened. But mostly we want to put the spotlight back on the band and their music because for decades they have been bringing out the kind emotions that got this whole thing started. Give it a listen and enjoy the music. Again. - Felix This podcast episode was produced by Noah Caldwell and edited by Jacob Ganz and Otis Hart. Suraya Mohamed is the executive producer of NPR Music. pages.text: Love classic cars? These are the most retro road trips on Earth | National Geographic TRAVEL Love classic cars? These are the most retro road trips on Earth Freedom, flexibility and a non-stop backdrop of epic views — there’s nothing quite like a road trip, and even better when it’s from the comfort of a classic car. Classic car tours are the pinnacle of slow-lane luxury, with vintage vehicles and cinematic roads to choose from. Photograph by Turo By Connor McGovern Published November 15, 2025 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Nothing beats hitting the open road. There’s something undeniably romantic about watching a destination roll by — all on your own schedule — and if you’ve opted for a convertible, the age-old cliche of feeling ‘the wind in your hair’ can become an exhilarating reality. Trend reports from the likes of Travelbag and Travel Tomorrow cite ‘slow travel’ as an enduring trend this year, where travellers take things a little more leisurely, focusing on the quality and depth of experiences rather than ticking off a list.
